[P1] 【标题】INCIDENT AT THE WINDOW
[P2] It chanced on Sunday, when Mr. Utterson was on his usual walk with Mr. Enfield, that their way lay once again through the by-street; and that when they came in front of the door, both stopped to gaze on it.
[P3] “Well,” said Enfield, “that story’s at an end at least. We shall never see more of Mr. Hyde.”
[P4] “I hope not,” said Utterson. “Did I ever tell you that I once saw him, and shared your feeling of repulsion?”
[P5] “It was impossible to do the one without the other,” returned Enfield. “And by the way, what an ass you must have thought me, not to know that this was a back way to Dr. Jekyll’s! It was partly your own fault that I found it out, even when I did.”
[P6] “So you found it out, did you?” said Utterson. “But if that be so, we may step into the court and take a look at the windows. To tell you the truth, I am uneasy about poor Jekyll; and even outside, I feel as if the presence of a friend might do him good.”
[P7] The court was very cool and a little damp, and full of premature twilight, although the sky, high up overhead, was still bright with sunset. The middle one of the three windows was half-way open; and sitting close beside it, taking the air with an infinite sadness of mien, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
[P8] “What! Jekyll! Jekyll!” he cried. “I trust you are better.”
[P9] “I am very low, Utterson,” replied the doctor drearily, “very low. It will not last long, thank God.”
[P10] “You stay too much indoors,” said the lawyer. “You should be out, whipping up the circulation like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now; get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”
[P11] “You are very good,” sighed the other. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is really a great pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place is really not fit.”
[P12] “Why, then,” said the lawyer, good-naturedly, “the best thing we can do is to stay down here and speak with you from where we are.”
[P13] “That is just what I was about to venture to propose,” returned the doctor with a smile. But the words were hardly uttered, before the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair, as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below. They saw it but for a glimpse for the window was instantly thrust down; but that glimpse had been sufficient, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they traversed the by-street; and it was not until they had come into a neighbouring thoroughfare, where even upon a Sunday there were still some stirrings of life, that Mr. Utterson at last turned and looked at his companion. They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.
[P14] “God forgive us, God forgive us,” said Mr. Utterson.
[P15] But Mr. Enfield only nodded his head very seriously, and walked on once more in silence.

[story_before_this_passage]
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.
最近事件：Utterson dines with Jekyll and Lanyon as inseparable friends.；Jekyll shuts his door against Utterson, Poole reporting he is confined.；Utterson visits Lanyon and is shocked by his decayed appearance.；Lanyon declares himself a doomed man who will never recover.；Lanyon refuses to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him.；Utterson writes to Jekyll, who replies of an incurable quarrel.；Jekyll vows extreme seclusion and speaks of an unnameable punishment.；Lanyon takes to his bed and dies within a fortnight.；After the funeral Utterson opens Lanyon's sealed envelope.；The enclosure is not to be opened till Jekyll's death or disappearance.；Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door rather than entering.；Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory and is silent.

[previous_passage_tail]
 long ago restored to its author, here again were the idea of a disappearance and the name of Henry Jekyll bracketed. But in the will, that idea had sprung from the sinister suggestion of the man Hyde; it was set there with a purpose all too plain and horrible. Written by the hand of Lanyon, what should it mean? A great curiosity came on the trustee, to disregard the prohibition and dive at once to the bottom of these mysteries; but professional honour and faith to his dead friend were stringent obligations; and the packet slept in the inmost corner of his private safe.
[P14] It is one thing to mortify curiosity, another to conquer it; and it may be doubted if, from that day forth, Utterson desired the society of his surviving friend with the same eagerness. He thought of him kindly; but his thoughts were disquieted and fearful. He went to call indeed; but he was perhaps relieved to be denied admittance; perhaps, in his heart, he preferred to speak with Poole upon the doorstep and surrounded by the air and sounds of the open city, rather than to be admitted into that house of voluntary bondage, and to sit and speak with its inscrutable recluse. Poole had, indeed, no very pleasant news to communicate. The doctor, it appeared, now more than ever confined himself to the cabinet over the laboratory, where he would sometimes even sleep; he was out of spirits, he had grown very silent, he did not read; it seemed as if he had something on his mind. Utterson became so used to the unvarying character of these reports, that he fell off little by little in the frequency of his visits.
